# Graph-Tree Representation Mismatch

Reference file for Dimension 4. All citations reference [citations.md](../citations.md). Updated 2026-04-19: academic citations [38][39][40] promoted from INACCESSIBLE to VERIFIED/PARTIAL via secondary sources and TU Eindhoven research portal; pattern count corrected (43 total, not "20+"); Cloudflare node-type count corrected (14, not 15).

## The Core Problem

Visual workflow editors present workflows as flat directed graphs (nodes + edges), while
execution engines often require nested tree structures (blocks containing blocks). This
mismatch creates a bidirectional transformation problem: the UI must convert between
representations whenever the user edits visually or the backend definition changes.

## Academic Foundations

### Process Structure Tree (PST)

The Refined Process Structure Tree decomposes a workflow graph into a hierarchy of
sub-workflows, each with a single entry and single exit point (SESE regions) [38]. This
decomposition:

- Can be computed in **linear time** using triconnected components [38]
- Is crucial for translating graph-based languages (BPMN) to block-structured languages
  (BPEL) [38]
- Maps directly to the flat-graph → nested-tree problem in workflow editors

### Workflow Control-Flow Patterns

Russell, ter Hofstede, van der Aalst, and Mulyar's "A Revised View" (2006) catalogues
**43 workflow control-flow patterns** — the 20 original patterns plus 23 newly identified
ones [40] (corrected 2026-04-19; prior research said "20+" which significantly
understated the count). Formal Coloured Petri-Net (CPN) descriptions are given for each,
and the paper evaluates implementation across 14 commercial systems (workflow engines,
BPM formalisms, BPEL). The NestFlow BPML work (Combi, Gambini, Migliorini, ADBIS 2011)
extends this taxonomy to cover hierarchical nesting through a small set of language
constructs [39]. These pattern catalogs provide the vocabulary for what a workflow editor
must be able to represent.

### DAG-to-Tree Conversion

The standard algorithm involves node duplication for nodes with multiple parents [38]:

1. Identify multi-parent nodes in the DAG
2. Duplicate nodes that have more than one incoming path
3. Each duplicate gets a single parent, producing a tree

The conversion is complete when every node has exactly one parent.

### Bidirectional Transformations

The academic literature on bidirectional transformations (lenses, bx) addresses the
view-update problem: how changes in one representation propagate to the other [38].
Key challenge: "flattening trees to lists is underspecified: many lists can be consistent
with the same tree."

## Industry Approaches

### Code-to-Graph (Cloudflare)

Cloudflare performs "static derivation of the graph" by analyzing TypeScript ASTs at
deployment time [18]. Their parser:

- Uses oxc-parser (OXC) via WebAssembly [18]
- Tracks Promise/await relationships to determine execution order [18]
- Defines **14 node types** (StepSleep, StepDo, StepWaitForEvent, StepSleepUntil, LoopNode, ParallelNode, TryNode, BlockNode, IfNode, SwitchNode, StartNode, FunctionCall, FunctionDef, BreakNode) [18] — corrected 2026-04-02 audit; prior research said 15
- Creates subgraphs for functions containing workflow steps [18]
- Handles loops (for...of, while, map, forEach), branching (switch/if/ternary),
  and parallel execution (unawaited promises, Promise.all) [18]

This is a **unidirectional** transformation (code → graph for visualization only).

### Code-First (Temporal)

Temporal argues explicitly against graph-based workflow definitions [10]:

| Problem | Graph Approach | Code Approach |
|---------|---------------|---------------|
| Dynamic control flow | "Router" nodes or runtime graph mutation [10] | Normal conditionals/loops [10] |
| Data passing | Global key-value store (untyped) or JSONPath [10] | Scoped variables with type safety [10] |
| Error handling | "Completely break down" — compensation paths create "unmanageable monstrosity" [10] | try/except blocks, compensation lists [10] |

Temporal's position: graphs "don't show the real control flow" hidden in expressions and
"cannot represent dynamic steps where critical logic often resides" [10]. Code with
OpenTelemetry tracing produces more accurate execution traces [10].

### Flat JSON (n8n)

n8n's workflow JSON uses a flat structure: a `nodes` array (configurations, parameters,
positions) and a `connections` object (workflow logic) [11]. The useCanvasMapping
composable bridges between n8n's internal `INodeUi` objects and Vue Flow's visual
Node objects [11].

### DAG-Based (Windmill, Airflow)

Windmill uses the OpenFlow JSON standard where "workflows are graphs (DAG) that represent
job specifications" [13]. Each step is code that produces results passed to dependent
steps [13]. Windmill uniquely supports both visual and code-based workflow definitions
outputting the same format [13].

Apache Airflow's core structure is a DAG: nodes are tasks, edges are dependencies [13].

## Transformation Strategies

| Strategy | Direction | Example |
|----------|-----------|---------|
| SESE decomposition | Graph → Tree | PST algorithm [38] |
| AST analysis | Code → Graph | Cloudflare workflow diagrams [18] |
| Bridge composable | Flat model ↔ Graph model | n8n useCanvasMapping [11] |
| Node duplication | DAG → Tree | Standard DAG-to-tree conversion [38] |
| Dual representation | Both maintained | Windmill visual + code [13] |

## When Graphs Fail

Temporal identifies specific failure cases [10]:

- Dynamic tool ordering in AI agents
- Parallel branch coordination requiring shared state
- Asynchronous event interruption of workflows
- Data-dependent compensations across multiple paths
- Complex reusability without explicit input/output contracts

## Additional Counter-Perspective

Beyond Temporal's critique [10], LangChain's Harrison Chase makes a complementary
argument [50]: "Visual workflow builders are not 'low' barrier to entry" and "complex
tasks quickly get too complicated to manage in a visual builder." Chase proposes a
three-tier alternative: low-complexity no-code agents (prompt + tools), medium-complexity
no-code workflows, and high-complexity code-based workflows using LangGraph. This is a
second vendor voice critiquing the flat-graph editor model — complementary to [10], from
a different angle (agent-focused rather than durable-execution-focused).

## Gaps and Limitations

- No published performance benchmarks for bidirectional transformation at scale
- Most industry implementations are unidirectional (code→graph or model→view)
- True bidirectional transformation (editing in either representation and syncing)
  remains largely an academic topic [38]
- The view-update problem is fundamentally underspecified for many graph structures
- Academic papers [34][35][38][39] are behind ACM/Springer paywalls; claims verified
  through secondary sources (conference coverage, author abstracts, preprint indexes)
  but specific implementation detail in these papers remains only partially verifiable
  without paid access. Graph-theoretic claims (linear time, SESE fragments, 43 patterns)
  are confirmed; narrower textual claims are not.
